title: OPEC+ Will Raise Output Targets for a Fourth Month. Almost None of It Will Reach the Market.
excerpt: The cartel meets today to approve another 188,000-barrel increase for July, but actual production has collapsed by nearly 10 million barrels a day since the Strait of Hormuz closed in February
body:
OPEC+ is set to approve a fourth consecutive monthly increase in oil output targets when seven of its core members meet on Sunday — a decision that, under normal circumstances, would signal confidence in the global economy. These are not normal circumstances. The targets are fiction.

The group of seven — Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan, Russia, and Oman — is expected to raise quotas by approximately 188,000 barrels per day for July, three OPEC+ sources told Reuters. That would bring the cumulative increase since April to nearly 800,000 barrels per day on paper.

In practice, the group's actual production has moved in the opposite direction. Output averaged 33.19 million barrels per day in April, down from 42.77 million in February, according to OPEC's own figures — a collapse of nearly 10 million barrels per day. The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil once flowed, has been effectively closed to most commercial traffic since Iran shut it on February 28. The United States responded with its own blockade in April. Over 1,500 vessels and approximately 22,500 mariners remain stranded.

The gap between what OPEC+ says it will produce and what it can actually deliver is the widest in the cartel's history.

The UAE Rupture

The crisis has already fractured the alliance. The United Arab Emirates left the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries after almost 60 years, a departure that forced adjustments to the monthly quota increases — the June and July hikes were trimmed from 206,000 to 188,000 barrels per day to account for the UAE's exit. A full OPEC+ ministerial meeting is also scheduled for Sunday but is not expected to make any policy changes, the sources said.

The UAE's departure underscores a deeper tension within the group. Member states with spare capacity — primarily Saudi Arabia and Russia — want to keep quota hikes on the books to signal stability and maintain market confidence. But the members most affected by the Hormuz closure, including Kuwait and Iraq, cannot physically export more oil regardless of what the quotas say.

The Inventory Alarm

The more pressing concern for global markets is not what OPEC+ decides on quotas but what is happening to oil inventories. In the United States, crude stockpiles including the Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 791 million barrels in the last week of May — the lowest since February 2024. American reserves have dropped by nearly 64 million barrels since the start of the war, declining for eight consecutive weeks.

The US is currently releasing 172 million barrels from the SPR as part of a coordinated International Energy Agency effort to release a record 400 million barrels globally. China's retreat from seaborne crude imports — which hit the lowest level in nearly a decade in May — has helped absorb some of the shock. But JPMorgan's Data Assets and Alpha group warned that these buffers are finite.

"Once we move into the back half of June it is likely that we see oil prices rapidly appreciate" unless Hormuz throughput normalises to pre-conflict levels, the bank said. Brent crude traded at approximately $93 per barrel as of June 5, down from a spike above $120 in March but still well above the sub-$70 levels that prevailed before the war.

"I think the risk of a second price shock is real, but the key point is that it may come from the exhaustion of buffers rather than from the initial Hormuz closure itself," said Shohruh Zukhritdinov, a Dubai-based oil trader.

What It Means for India

India, the world's third-largest oil importer, has already been reshaping its supply chains at speed. Venezuelan oil is on track to make Caracas India's fourth-largest crude supplier. Imports from Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria have risen sharply. Russian oil continues to flow at roughly 1.9 million barrels per day, albeit at a 425 percent premium above pre-war prices.

But the structural shift is costly. Nuvama Institutional Equities warned last week that the combination of an oil shock and a potentially weak monsoon raises the risk of stagflation for the Indian economy in FY27, even as FY26 closed with headline growth of 7.7 percent. The brokerage revised its growth forecast downward to 6 to 6.5 percent.

Northern Trust Asset Management's chief investment strategist, Joseph Tanious, put the new reality bluntly: "The Strait of Hormuz is now firmly established as a persistent geopolitical chokepoint." A return to pre-war oil prices below $70 looks unlikely even if tensions ease, he added.

For Indian households already dealing with elevated fuel and cooking oil costs, the question is not whether OPEC+ approves another quota increase. It is whether the world's oil buffers hold long enough for diplomacy to catch up with the market.

Rosneft CEO Igor Sechin said at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum that oil markets could realign with fundamentals by the second half of 2027 — if the crisis is resolved. For now, the word "if" carries a $93 price tag.
